newsitem.title: RUSSIA: RUSSIA WON'T GIVE ALL BANKS SECURITIES LICENCE. [CORRECTED 12:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: RUSSIA WON'T GIVE ALL BANKS SECURITIES LICENCE. [CORRECTED 12:50 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects headline and text to make clear that Kozlov was talking only of securities market licences for banks, not general licences)

The Central Bank of Russia will not give securities market licences to all commercial banks when it issues them to the industry at the start of next year, a senior central bank official said on Tuesday.
"There are those banks with no problems, those with occasional problems, those with just problems and those with enormous problems," Deputy Chairman Andrei Kozlov said.
"Now we would like to exclude the lower strata," he told Reuters. "It's my estimate there are a couple of hundred nearly dead banks."
Kozlov said the central bank was likely to give securities licences to only 1,400-1,500 of Russia's 1,900 banks.
He stressed this was a personal estimate, as detailed work on which banks fall into which category was still to be done.
Under a recent agreement on regulating Russian securities markets, the Central Bank will licence commercial banks from January 1 next year.
Kozlov said the Federal Commission for the Securities Market, which has overall responsibility for regulating the markets, was drawing up new rules likely to be ready in September.

The Central Bank, which regulates the banking sector on behalf of the Commission, would start issuing new licences once these rules were ready. Commission and Bank officials agreed last Thursday that not all banks would get a licence, he said.
The Central Bank already licences commercial banks, and in recent years has been gradually reducing their number.
Many Russian banks are not banks in the Western sense, but small undercapitalised institutions set up to speculate in Russia's once chaotic financial markets.

With the stabilisation of the rouble in 1995, and the fall in government securities yields since last summer, which Kozlov said was set to continue, such banks' opportunities for easy trading profits have evaporated and they have little chance of surviving.
